subject: Cooking
title: Fermentation and Climate Change
description: Learn Fermentation and Climate Change in one minute.

hook.text: Fermentation could help solve climate change. Not with cars — with food.

buildup.text: Livestock produces 14.5% of global greenhouse gases. Fermented plant-based proteins could replace much of it.

discovery.text: Mycoprotein (Quorn) is grown by fermenting fungus — producing protein with 90% less land than beef.

twist.text: Fermentation can also upcycle food waste — turning brewery grain, fruit pulp, and vegetable scraps into new products.

climax.text: Startups are using fermentation to create palm oil alternatives, eliminating a major driver of deforestation.

punchline.text: The oldest food technology might save the newest food crisis.

quiz.question: How much less land does mycoprotein production require compared to beef?

details.summary: Fermentation could help address climate change by reducing food waste through preservation, replacing resource-intensive animal agriculture with precision-fermented proteins, and enabling carbon capture by microorganisms.
details.whyItMatters: As climate concerns reshape food systems, fermentation offers both ancient preservation wisdom and cutting-edge biotechnology solutions. Its role in sustainable food production is growing rapidly.
takeaways: Fermentation extends food shelf life, reducing waste significantly
Precision-fermented proteins use a fraction of agricultural resources
Industrial fermentation's own carbon footprint needs monitoring

faq.question: How does fermentation reduce food waste?
faq.answer: Fermentation preserves perishable foods for months or years without refrigeration. Surplus vegetables become sauerkraut, excess fruit becomes wine or vinegar, and surplus grain becomes beer or bread. Before refrigeration, fermentation was the primary method of preventing food spoilage.

faq.question: Can fermentation replace animal agriculture?
faq.answer: Precision fermentation can produce dairy proteins, egg proteins, and fats without animals. This uses roughly 90 percent less land and water than traditional dairy farming. Full replacement is decades away, but fermented alternatives are already entering the market.
